newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia hopes for permanent Yugo assets freeze.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia hopes for permanent Yugo assets freeze.

text.p: Slovenia said on Monday it expected to convince a Nicosia court to keep Yugoslav deposits in Cyprus frozen until the end of succession talks between the former republics of Yugoslavia.

Some deposits of Yugoslavia offshore bank Beogradska Banka in Cyprus have been temporarily frozen since July after Slovenia argued that the former National Bank of Yugoslavia had about $146 million on the account of the Cyprus-based bank.

"We believe our arguments are sound enough to convince the court in Cyprus to permanently freeze the assets until the succession talks are finished," Andrej Rant, the president of the management board of the Slovenian Succession Fund, told Reuters.
He said the court hearing, which started at the end of July, would continue in Nicosia on Tuesday.
The Beogradska bank has rejected Slovenia's claim.
When Slovenia was part of Yugoslavia, it was obliged to deposit its foreign exchange in the Yugoslav central bank, which subsequently deposited it in banks abroad.
According to Slovenian estimates, various banks, among them Beogradska's branch on Cyprus, hold about $1.2 billion of the former Yugoslavia's assets.
About $660 million of those assets are held in the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) which froze them after the breakup of former Yugoslavia in 1991.

The Basle-based BIS recently suggested the assets held by the BIS should be divided according to a plan introduced by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) which would give Slovenia a 16.39 percent stake.
Governors of the central banks of Slovenia, Macedonia, Croatia and Bosnia have all said they supported the BIS proposal, while rump Yugoslavia has so far refused to participate in the negotiations.

Rump Yugoslavia, now comprising Serbia and Montenegro, has also attempted to torpedo other successor republics' moves to settle their shares of the former Yugoslavia's commercial debt, estimated at $4.3 billion.
Both Slovenia and Croatia have ignored legal challenges by Belgrade and completed separate rescheduling agreements with their creditors.
